blocks.text: 我们发布 SWE-2.1，这是对 SWE-2 的一次重大升级。与前代一样，它在 Kimi K3 上通过纯强化学习训练而成。在 FrontierCode 2.0、Terminal-Bench 4.1 等众多基准测试中，它都取得了大幅提升。我们之所以能在编码性能上获得大部分增益，是因为瞄准了通用智能和长时程工作流。这也带动了其他多个领域的进步，尤其是网络安全。

blocks.text: 网络安全

inlines.text: 网络安全

blocks.text: 训练带来的一个显著提升，是模型在网络安全、漏洞发现与利用任务上的能力大幅增强。SWE-2.1 在 ExploitBench 上达到 80%，在 ExploitGym 上通过预期利用手法捕获了 27.3% 的 flag。可见该模型不仅擅长发现漏洞，还能走完整个利用链，往往需要数小时的自主工作。

inlines.text: 保障训练基础设施安全

blocks.text: 训练一个具备先进网络安全能力的模型，需要额外的防护措施。因此，我们在训练中内置了多项安全机制：

inlines.text: 训练一个具备先进网络安全能力的模型，需要额外的防护措施。因此，我们在训练中内置了多项安全机制：
我们对训练环境进行了红队测试，重点针对沙箱。
我们实施了持续的安全监控。我们设计了一项金丝雀评估，让模型尝试逃出沙箱；一旦成功，基础设施就会向研究人员发出警报。

blocks.text: 这项金丝雀评估是一项成功的干预措施。即便经过大量红队测试，模型在训练期间仍四次发现了我们沙箱中的新漏洞。每次研究人员都收到警报并立即作出响应。

blocks.text: 防护措施与防御方访问

inlines.text: 防护措施与防御方访问

blocks.text: 由于先进能力（尤其是网络安全领域）存在被滥用的风险，我们在部署 SWE-2.1 时配备了防护措施，用于检测并阻止最危险的行为。这些措施针对的是一小类高危害活动，并经过校准，确保大多数合法工作（包括网络防御工作）不受影响。

inlines.text: 数据与训练配方

blocks.text: 为了训练 SWE-2.1，我们扩展了任务和环境，覆盖短时程和长时程两类工作流，涉及从科学、性能工程到网络安全的多个领域。这种广度让模型更加多才多艺，也把它的软件工程表现推得更高。

inlines.text: 为了训练 SWE-2.1，我们扩展了任务和环境，覆盖短时程和长时程两类工作流，涉及从科学、性能工程到网络安全的多个领域。这种广度让模型更加多才多艺，也把它的软件工程表现推得更高。

blocks.text: 我们还改进了后训练算法，以便在训练中控制 rollout 长度。此前，长度振荡常常破坏训练动态的稳定性。减少这些振荡后，我们就能在从几分钟到数小时不等的任务上稳定训练。

blocks.text: We’re releasing SWE-2.1, a major upgrade over SWE-2. Like its predecessor, it is trained with pure reinforcement learning on Kimi K3. It delivers large gains across a wide range of benchmarks including FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench 4.1. We achieve much of our gains in coding performance by targeting general intelligence and long-horizon workflows. This also leads to improvements across a variety of other domains, especially cybersecurity.

blocks.text: Cybersecurity

inlines.text: Cybersecurity

blocks.text: One notable improvement through our training is significantly increased capability on cybersecurity, vulnerability finding and exploitation tasks. SWE-2.1 achieves 80% on ExploitBench and 27.3% flags captured via intended exploits on ExploitGym. The model thus shows strong performance not only in finding vulnerabilities, but also carrying them out through the full exploitation chain, often over several hours of autonomous work.

blocks.text: Securing training infrastructure

inlines.text: Securing training infrastructure

blocks.text: Training a model with advanced capabilities in cybersecurity requires additional safeguards. Therefore, we built several security measures into training:

inlines.text: Training a model with advanced capabilities in cybersecurity requires additional safeguards. Therefore, we built several security measures into training:
We red-teamed our training setup, particularly around sandboxes.
We implemented continuous safety monitoring. We created a canary eval where the model tries to escape the sandbox. Upon success, our infrastructure alerts the researchers.

blocks.text: The canary eval has been a successful intervention. Even after extensive red-teaming, the model discovered new vulnerabilities in our sandbox four times during training. Researchers were alerted and responded immediately each time.

blocks.text: Safeguards and access for defenders

inlines.text: Safeguards and access for defenders

blocks.text: Because advanced capabilities, particularly in cybersecurity, carry a risk of misuse, we deployed SWE-2.1 with safeguards that detect and prevent the most dangerous kinds of behavior. These safeguards target a narrow set of high-harm activities, and are calibrated to leave most legitimate work, including work in cyber defense, unaffected.

inlines.text: Because advanced capabilities, particularly in cybersecurity, carry a risk of misuse, we deployed SWE-2.1 with safeguards that detect and prevent the most dangerous kinds of behavior. These safeguards target a narrow set of high-harm activities, and are calibrated to leave most legitimate work, including work in cyber defense, unaffected.

blocks.text: At the same time, some advanced defensive work requires capabilities these safeguards restrict. AI is raising the floor for attackers: exploits that once required rare expertise are now within reach of anyone with a capable model. We want to give defenders the same leverage, so we are rolling out SWE-2.1 Cyber, a version of SWE-2.1 with more permissive safeguards, to Devin Security.

inlines.text: Data and Recipe

blocks.text: To train SWE-2.1, we expanded our tasks and environments across both short- and long-horizon workflows, spanning areas from science and performance engineering to cybersecurity. That breadth made the model more versatile while pushing its software engineering performance even further.

That breadth made the model more versatile while pushing its software engineering performance even further.

blocks.text: We also improved our post-training algorithms to control rollout length during training. Previously, length oscillations often destabilized training dynamics. Reducing those oscillations let us train reliably on tasks ranging from a few minutes to many hours.

blocks.text: Together, our data and recipe improvements allowed us to train stably for much longer, with performance on held-out eval tasks improving steadily throughout many days of training. This new recipe also contributed to SWE-2.1’s improved test-time scaling, helping SWE-2.1 make better use of additional compute on difficult tasks.

blocks.text: We are also releasing SWE-2.1 Lightning. Through a partnership with Cerebras, we are able to provide the same model at 10× the speed. Because SWE-2.1 continues to improve with more test-time compute, inference speed determines how much work it can finish under a tight deadline. During an active incident or urgent fix, 10× throughput turns hours of investigation and iteration into just minutes.

blocks.text: Benchmark Methodology Notes

inlines.text: Benchmark Methodology Notes

blocks.text: Harness: We report upstream or self-reported scores if they're available. Otherwise, we evaluate models on our internal evaluation framework. For closed models, we use the model developer's preferred harness. For open and SWE models, we use the Devin CLI harness.

inlines.text: Harness:

We report upstream or self-reported scores if they're available. Otherwise, we evaluate models on our internal evaluation framework. For closed models, we use the model developer's preferred harness. For open and SWE models, we use the Devin CLI harness.

blocks.text: Time budgets: To keep benchmark scores independent of inference speed, we enforce time limits on a simulated clock that charges each model call 1 s of time-to-first-token plus a constant c seconds per output token (a fixed TPS), matching our production serving speeds: time in seconds=turns+c×tokens+tools.

inlines.text: Time budgets:

To keep benchmark scores independent of inference speed, we enforce time limits on a simulated clock that charges each model call 1 s of time-to-first-token plus a constant c seconds per output token (a fixed TPS), matching our production serving speeds: time in seconds=turns+c×tokens+tools.

blocks.text: ProgramBench: We report the percentage of tasks where the model passes at least 95% of tests. SWE-2.1 and SWE-2 are run in our harness with a 250k-token context with up to 3 compactions (1M tokens total). Other models are reported in mini-swe-agent with each model's native context window (up to ~1M tokens).

inlines.text: ProgramBench:

We report the percentage of tasks where the model passes at least 95% of tests. SWE-2.1 and SWE-2 are run in our harness with a 250k-token context with up to 3 compactions (1M tokens total). Other models are reported in mini-swe-agent with each model's native context window (up to ~1M tokens).

blocks.text: ExploitBench: We ran each task five times with a 3-hour simulated clock and took the union of the flags captured for each task. Taking the union of flags is standard practice for this benchmark (see e.g. the GPT-5.6 System Card).

blocks.text: ExploitGym: We report pass@1 over the set of 869 tasks within a 6-hour timeout. We evaluate with mitigations disabled, following Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Neon. We report two metrics - flags captured and success, following the ExploitGym paper. “Flags captured” includes successful, real exploits unrelated to the intended vulnerability specified in the initial prompt. To compute “success”, we adopted the upstream agent-as-a-judge implementation.

inlines.text: ExploitGym:

We report pass@1 over the set of 869 tasks within a 6-hour timeout. We evaluate with mitigations disabled, following Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Neon. We report two metrics - flags captured and success, following the ExploitGym paper. “Flags captured” includes successful, real exploits unrelated to the intended vulnerability specified in the initial prompt. To compute “success”, we adopted the upstream agent-as-a-judge implementation.
